parts.title: The Science Of Shopping
parts.article:
A You may have wondered why so many supermarkets are virtually indistinguishable from each other. It is not, as some might suspect, that the companies operating them lack imagination. It is more that they are all well-versed in the science of persuading people to buy things - a science that, thanks to technological advances, is beginning to understand what motivates consumers when they make decisions on what to purchase.

B It takes a while for the mind to get into a shopping mode. People need to make a gentle start and take stock of the surroundings. This is why some supermarkets have a so-called chill zone for browsing magazines, books and DVDs, an area which is also designed to catch the customer's eye and tempt them to make impulsive purchases. But many will ignore it, in which case the first thing they encounter is the fresh fruit and vegetables section. For shoppers, this makes no sense. Fruit in particular can be easily bruised, so ideally should be bought at the end, not the beginning, of a shopping trip. But psychology is at work here: selecting wholesome fresh food is an uplifting way to start shopping, and it makes people feel less guilty about reaching for the less nutritious stuff later on.

C Shoppers have worked out that everyday items, like milk, will invariably be placed in an aisle towards the back of a store to provide more opportunity to tempt customers on their way there. This is also why pharmacies are generally at the rear, even in convenience stores. But supermarkets know shoppers know this, so they use other tricks, like placing popular items halfway along a section, thereby forcing people to walk along the aisle looking for them. The idea is to boost the length of time shoppers spend in a store.

D Having walked to the end of the fruit and vegetable aisle, shoppers arrive at counters of prepared food, the fishmonger and the butcher. Then there is the in-store bakery, which can be smelt before being seen. Even small supermarkets now use in-store bakeries. Mostly these bake pre-prepared items, and they have boomed, although central bakeries that deliver to many stores are more efficient. The smell of freshly baked bread can make people hungry, encouraging them to buy not just bread but other food.

E There are also numerous ways stores get shoppers to choose particular products. For example, stores encourage customers to buy expensive branded products by arranging them at eye-level, with cheaper ones lower down. Often head offices specify where everything has to be placed and spot-checks are carried out to make sure instructions are followed to the letter. But shelf-positioning is extremely controversial. Despite all the academic papers written on how best to stack shelves, retailers have their own views. While many stores consider eye-level to be the top spot, others think a little higher is better.

F Technology is making the process of monitoring shopper behaviour easier, which is why the security cameras in stores may be doing considerably more than watching out for theft. Pictures showing shoppers while they are making their selections can now be analysed. It is possible to see how many shoppers went straight to one brand, the number that hesitated, and those that compared several brands. However, despite the availability of sophisticated technology, researchers have found that simply talking to consumers as they exit the store can yield valuable insights. This low-tech approach has become widespread following comments from stores that data collected electronically tells them little about why so many customers leave without making a purchase. Face-to-face interviews reveal that customers leave shops empty-handed more often because they are unable to decide than because prices are too high.

G People tell market researchers that they make decisions about what to buy based on logic and common sense, considering issues such as price, quality or convenience. But there are clearly other factors which play a role, such as certain feelings and memories which individuals are not fully aware of. Researchers hired by big stores are now conducting studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging, which detects changes in the brain corresponding to increases or decreases in mental activity. Research participants are shown different products and asked questions about them, while scanners reveal their brain activity as they respond. Often, major contradictions are apparent between what they say and what they are thinking. This is immensely valuable information. Eight out of ten new consumer products launched on the market do not succeed, despite having been tested on people who insist they would buy them but who, deep down, may have reservations about the desirability of these products.

H This shopping science probably has its limits, however. Dr Eric Spangenberg of the University of Washington argues that while it's unlikely that someone could be persuaded to buy something they don't need, they might be convinced to choose one brand in preference to another without being aware that this is happening. This claim is also borne out by numerous research findings. But if consumers were to realise quite how much research is being done into the many psychological factors influencing their choices, they might be much more wary of making purchases in the future.
parts.questions:
Questions 27–30
Choose the correct answer.

Q27 What does the writer suggest about supermarkets in the first paragraph?

  • A They need to try harder to be different from one another.
  • B They share a similar understanding of consumer psychology.
  • C They depend too much on the latest technology.
  • D They should do more to analyse how consumers think.

Q28 The writer says the function of the ‘chill zone’ in supermarkets is

  • A to give customers time to decide what they want to buy.
  • B to present customers with a range of interesting bargains.
  • C to ensure customers feel under no pressure to buy anything.
  • D to help customers slowly prepare themselves to go shopping.

Q29 According to the writer, placing fruit and vegetables near the front of the store

  • A ensures the customers will feel good about the first products they buy.
  • B reduces the risk of customers damaging these products later on.
  • C encourages customers to buy more of these products than they intended.
  • D makes customers consider healthier options in other sections they visit.

Q30 What point does the writer make about shoppers in the third paragraph?

  • A They spend more time in stores than they realise.
  • B They believe stores make life unnecessarily difficult for them.
  • C They are aware of some of the techniques used by stores.
  • D They are confused by frequent changes in the layout of stores.
Questions 31–35
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 31–35 on your answer sheet, write:

Q31 Cheaper products are placed on lower shelves to minimise the likelihood that they will be bought.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q32 Head offices should be more flexible about how products are arranged by supermarkets.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q33 There is widespread agreement on how products should be arranged on shelves.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q34 Security cameras are a serious threat to customers' privacy.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q35 Technology is the best tool for determining why shoppers fail to make purchases.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 36–40
Complete the summary using the list of words and phrases, A-I, below.
New technology could help retailers sell more
Research is providing insights into what makes people purchase particular products. Most shoppers believe that their choices are the result of . Research involving fMRI scanners, however, has revealed that certain influence shoppers' decisions to a significant extent. In the research, a comparison was made between participants' stated opinions of a product and data from , which often indicated a radically different . As most new products are , this data could be extremely valuable for marketing departments.
  • A brain scans

Q27

解析 第一段指出，超市看起来都一样，是因为它们都精通说服人们购物的科学，也就是分享着相似的消费心理学。

干扰 你可能想选A，但作者只是陈述超市看起来无法区分这一事实，并没有建议它们需要努力变得与众不同。

句子 A You may have wondered why so many supermarkets are virtually indistinguishable from each other. It is not, as some might suspect, that the companies operating them lack imagination. It is more that they are all well-versed in the science of persuading people to buy things - a science that, thanks to technological advances, is beginning to understand what motivates consumers when they make decisions on what to purchase.

Q28

解析 大脑需要时间进入购物模式，所以“休闲区”的作用是让顾客平缓地开始，慢慢为购物做好准备。

干扰 你可能想选A（给顾客时间决定买什么），但原文强调的是让顾客在心理上进入状态，而不是让他们在休闲区里构思具体的购物清单。

句子 B It takes a while for the mind to get into a shopping mode. People need to make a gentle start and take stock of the surroundings. This is why some supermarkets have a so-called chill zone for browsing magazines, books and DVDs, an area which is also designed to catch the customer's eye and tempt them to make impulsive purchases.

Q29

解析 把新鲜果蔬放在最前面是一种心理战术，能让顾客在刚开始购物时就感到身心愉悦，减少后续买不健康食品的罪恶感。

干扰 你可能想选B（减少损坏风险），但原文明确指出，从保护水果的角度看放在最前面其实更容易在后续购物中被压坏，因此这完全是出于心理层面的考虑。

句子 For shoppers, this makes no sense. Fruit in particular can be easily bruised, so ideally should be bought at the end, not the beginning, of a shopping trip. But psychology is at work here: selecting wholesome fresh food is an uplifting way to start shopping, and it makes people feel less guilty about reaching for the less nutritious stuff later on.

Q30

解析 第三段明确指出，顾客已经看透了超市把日常必需品放在店面深处来诱惑他们的套路。

干扰 你可能想选A（花的时间比意识到的长），但这只是超市布局想达到的目的，本段的核心重点是顾客对超市的这些套路是知情的。

句子 C Shoppers have worked out that everyday items, like milk, will invariably be placed in an aisle towards the back of a store to provide more opportunity to tempt customers on their way there. This is also why pharmacies are generally at the rear, even in convenience stores. But supermarkets know shoppers know this, so they use other tricks, like placing popular items halfway along a section, thereby forcing people to walk along the aisle looking for them.

Q31

解析 原文说把便宜商品放在下面是为了凸显和鼓励顾客购买放在视线平齐处的昂贵商品，而不是为了尽量不让人买便宜商品。

干扰 你可能会顺着题目逻辑觉得合理，但原文明确指出了这种摆放的真正动机（鼓励买贵的），这与题目所说的动机（减少买便宜的）相违背。

句子 E There are also numerous ways stores get shoppers to choose particular products. For example, stores encourage customers to buy expensive branded products by arranging them at eye-level, with cheaper ones lower down.

Q32

解析 原文只提到了总部会严格规定商品的摆放位置并进行抽查，但完全没有表达总部“应该更加灵活”这种观点。

干扰 你可能看到原文说摆放位置“有争议”，就脑补出作者建议总部要灵活，但在做题时，没提到的建议坚决不能选。

句子 Often head offices specify where everything has to be placed and spot-checks are carried out to make sure instructions are followed to the letter. But shelf-positioning is extremely controversial. Despite all the academic papers written on how best to stack shelves, retailers have their own views.

Q33

解析 原文明确指出货架摆放是“极具争议的”，且各家零售商看法不一，直接反驳了题目中的“达成广泛共识”。

干扰 题目中的“达成共识”和原文的“极具争议”是反义词，只要抓住这个核心冲突就能快速判断。

句子 But shelf-positioning is extremely controversial. Despite all the academic papers written on how best to stack shelves, retailers have their own views. While many stores consider eye-level to be the top spot, others think a little higher is better.

Q34

解析 原文提到了监控摄像头可以用来分析顾客的购物行为，但完全没有提到这是否会对顾客的“隐私”造成严重威胁。

干扰 你可能会根据常识觉得摄像头必然侵犯隐私，但记住一定要基于原文给出的信息做判断，不能带入个人常识。

句子 F Technology is making the process of monitoring shopper behaviour easier, which is why the security cameras in stores may be doing considerably more than watching out for theft. Pictures showing shoppers while they are making their selections can now be analysed.

Q35

解析 原文明确指出电子数据（高科技）几乎无法说明顾客为什么不买东西就离开，反而简单的面对面交流（低科技）更有效。

干扰 题目说科技是“最好”的工具，但原文直接说明了收集来的电子数据在分析顾客为何不购买时其实用处极小。

句子 However, despite the availability of sophisticated technology, researchers have found that simply talking to consumers as they exit the store can yield valuable insights. This low-tech approach has become widespread following comments from stores that data collected electronically tells them little about why so many customers leave without making a purchase.

Q36

解析 原文说人们告诉研究人员，他们的决定是基于逻辑和常识的，这直接对应了选项G的“理性的决定”。

干扰 原文中的 logic and common sense（逻辑和常识）完美等价于选项里的 rational decisions，找准这个对应就不会错。

句子 G People tell market researchers that they make decisions about what to buy based on logic and common sense, considering issues such as price, quality or convenience.

Q37

解析 原文说人们的决定还会受到一些自己都没有完全意识到的感觉和记忆的影响，这对应选项C的“无意识因素”。

干扰 不要被后文复杂的扫描仪技术带偏，答案就藏在 not fully aware of（没有完全意识到）这个表达里，它直接对应了 unconscious。

句子 But there are clearly other factors which play a role, such as certain feelings and memories which individuals are not fully aware of. Researchers hired by big stores are now conducting studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging, which detects changes in the brain corresponding to increases or decreases in mental activity.

Q38

解析 研究中，参与者会被提问（表达自身看法），同时扫描仪会揭示他们的大脑活动，这直接对应选项A的“大脑扫描”。

干扰 题目要求找的是和“顾客声称的意见”作对比的数据来源，原文清晰指出了扫描仪看到的大脑活动是对比物，不要填错成其他的干扰项。

句子 Research participants are shown different products and asked questions about them, while scanners reveal their brain activity as they respond.

Q39

解析 扫描仪的数据经常显示，人们嘴上说的和心里真实的内心活动往往存在巨大矛盾，这说明数据揭示了截然不同的“情感反应（选项H）”。

干扰 这道题需要稍微往深层理解，原文用“心里想的”来指代更真实的情绪和保留意见，所以对应了情感反应，不要硬找完全一模一样的原词。

句子 Research participants are shown different products and asked questions about them, while scanners reveal their brain activity as they respond. Often, major contradictions are apparent between what they say and what they are thinking.

Q40

解析 原文提到十分之八的新消费产品在市场上都没有成功，这直接对应了选项E的“失败产品”。

干扰 原文的 do not succeed 就是 failures 的直白表达，看懂这层对应就能迅速锁定答案。

句子 This is immensely valuable information. Eight out of ten new consumer products launched on the market do not succeed, despite having been tested on people who insist they would buy them but who, deep down, may have reservations about the desirability of these products.
